records.artist_dates: Born at Leiden in 1468; died at Leiden in 1533.
records.title: A Knight (Charles V) on Horseback
records.lender: Lent by The Worcester Art Museum.
records.note: The composition, especially that of the horse, is influenced by Dürer's engraving, Knight, Death and the Devil (1513). Dr. Janson pointed out that the figure on horseback probably represents Charles V and that the painting was executed soon after the Emperor's successful campaign in Tunis in 1535. This would preclude the likelihood that Engelbrechtsz, who died in 1533, is the author of the painting. While his deduction is convincing, his attribution to Jan Vermeyen is impossible for stylistic reasons. G. J. Hoogewerff is probably correct in giving the painting to Cornelis Cornelisz, the second son of Engelbrechtsz (1493-1544). (De Noord-Nederlandsche Schilderkunst, 1939, III, p. 204). The painting is closely related to Engelbrechtsz to whom it has been attributed by Friedländer and others, but shows a slight difference in style which can be explained by accepting an execution in Engelbrechtsz' workshop, which was taken over by Cornelis Cornelisz after his father's death. COLLECTIONS: Hilder; Crawford; Samuel Rogers; Earl of Northbrook. DESCRIBED: Friedländer, op. cit., X, No. 108; Horst W. Janson, Worcester Art Museum Annual, Vol. I, 1935-36, pp. 19-31.
records.collections: Hilder; Crawford; Samuel Rogers; Earl of Northbrook.

records.artist_dates: Born at Leiden in 1495; died in England in 1552.
records.title: Lot and his Daughters
records.lender: The Detroit Institute of Arts (Purchased 1925).
records.note: A forged Lucas van Leyden signature with the date 1523 proved to be a later addition which disappeared in a recent cleaning. This false signature has been accepted by two scholars, N. Beets (Oud Holland, Vol. 53, 1936, p. 63) and G. J. Hoogewerff (op. cit., III, p. 352) who had not seen the original, as argument that the present painting and the group of paintings by the same master must be the work of Lucas Cornelisz. These paintings had formerly been attributed by Friedländer to Jan de Cock (Jan Wellens de Cock of Leiden; member of the Guild at Antwerp in 1503; died there about 1527). The basis of Friedländer's attribution was an engraving of about 1550 after a St. Christopher in the Bissing Collection, by our artist. This engraving is signed J. Kock C. Dankertz exc. and above these names is the word pictum. Beets and Hoogewerff believe these are the names of the editors and that the artist's name (before pictum) disappeared in the later states of the print, which are the only ones still in existence. In any case, the date and the close connection of this painting and others by the same artist with the atelier of Engelbrechtsz point to identification with Lucas Cornelisz. A painting in the Vienna museum (No. 652a) closely related to ours, is a partial copy after the Pieta in Engelbrechtsz's triptych in Leiden, which was executed about 1515-1520. The copy could hardly be earlier than 1520; this would coincide with the dates of Lucas Cornelisz but not with those of Jan Wellens de Cock, who at this time had lived in Antwerp for many years. Several small portraits also, one of which is signed with the name of Lucas Cornelisz and represents Sir Thomas Wyatt the Elder, correspond with the style of Engelbrechtsz who lived in England in later life.

catalogue_author.as_printed: CATALOGUE BY W. R. VALENTINER (title page: LOAN EXHIBITION OF EARLY DUTCH PAINTINGS 1460-1540 — THE DETROIT INSTITUTE OF ARTS — TWENTY-FIFTH LOAN EXHIBITION — February, 1944). The pamphlet nowhere states Valentiner's directorship of the Institute; no role beyond catalogue authorship is printed.

introduction.as_printed: INTRODUCTION (printed pp. 1–7 of the catalogue; unsigned as printed). A survey of Dutch painting of the fifteenth and early sixteenth centuries by school — Haarlem, Amsterdam, Leiden, Delft, Hertogenbosch, Utrecht — discussing many of the exhibited pictures by catalogue number.

apparatus.lenders_note: The LENDERS TO THE EXHIBITION page (16 lenders) as printed. Every lender in the list lends at least one work in the catalogue, and every entry's lender line resolves to a name in the list (audit, Nov 25, 2026).
apparatus.artist_essays: Each artist heading in the catalogue body is followed by a short biographical essay as printed; the heading and the life dates stated in the essay head are captured on each record (artist_heading, artist_dates). The essays themselves are not transcribed.
notes: The catalogue prints no separate checklist: the numbered catalogue body (printed pp. 8–15) is the whole run, nos. 1–27, complete with no gaps or duplicates, followed by the twelve plate leaves; the remaining pages of this copy are blank. The intake inventory's mention of a closing checklist is not borne out by the scan.
Entry numbers are printed in an old-style serif in which the numeral 1 resembles a Roman 'I'; they are read as Arabic numerals throughout, consistently with the plate captions.
No. 2: the DESCRIBED line cites W. R. Valentiner's Art Quarterly article as treating “Aelbert van Outwater” (sic), against the heading's OUWATER. As printed.

No. 13: the note's last sentence reads that the small portraits “correspond with the style of Engelbrechtsz who lived in England in later life” — as printed; on the catalogue's own essay it was Lucas Cornelisz who went to England (about 1527) and died there in 1552.
No. 24: the COLLECTIONS line prints “Lady Purbright. London” with a full stop after Purbright, as printed.
No. 26: the note prints “characterisic” (sic) for “characteristic”. As printed.

No. 11 stands under the heading CORNELIS ENGELBRECHTSZ as printed, although the entry's own note argues the picture is probably by his son Cornelis Cornelisz in the Engelbrechtsz workshop; the heading attribution is the record, the argument is in the note.
The lender lines print “Galleries” (The Schaeffer Galleries, The Silberman Galleries) — the spelling is as printed throughout, as is “Kleinberger Galleries” in no. 6's EXHIBITED line.
